points: National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland, published in 2016: the government's plan to increase physical activity levels across the population, with actions across health, education, transport, sport and communities.

notes.h: National and local bodies and local actions
points: Sport Ireland: the statutory body responsible for developing sport in Ireland, established in 2015 under the Sport Ireland Act 2015, replacing the Irish Sports Council.
Sport Ireland funds national governing bodies and Local Sports Partnerships, runs participation programmes and anti-doping, and supports high performance.
Local Sports Partnerships (LSPs): local bodies in counties and cities, funded by Sport Ireland, that increase participation at local level.
LSPs focus on under-represented groups and work through local programmes, coach education, community events and information.
County council recreation and active-travel plans, which provide greenways, parks and cycle lanes.
School physical activity policies, which set out how the school provides PE and activity.
Club development plans, which set out how a club will grow its membership and coaching.

notes.b: A named policy can be analysed through its aims, its actions, its target and its strengths and limitations. The example is the National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland.
points: Aim: to increase physical activity levels across the population.
Actions: set out across health, education, transport, sport and communities.
Target: the whole population, so several sectors of society have a role.
Strength: it coordinates action across government sectors, so health, education and transport are linked in one plan.
Strength: a national framework gives local bodies a shared direction.
Limitation: its actions depend on each sector implementing them, so gaps in implementation slow progress.
Limitation: funding gaps can stop local actions from going ahead.
Limitation: many local activities rely on volunteers, which limits how far they can grow.

notes.h: Tip sheet: target group and promotion tips
notes.b: A tip sheet names one target group, gives promotion tips to attract them and adherence tips to keep them taking part, and justifies each tip for that group.
points: Target group: choose one specific group, such as teenage girls, older adults, office workers or beginners returning after a long absence.
Promotion: start small with short, easy sessions, because a modest first step feels manageable and is more likely to be repeated.
Promotion: choose enjoyable activities, since people keep doing what they enjoy.
Promotion: exercise with friends or in a group, because shared activity adds social motivation.
Promotion: schedule activity like an appointment, so it is planned rather than left to chance.
Promotion: set a clear first goal, such as attending one session each week, so early success is visible from the start.
Promotion: use free local options such as parkrun, walking routes and greenways, which remove cost as a barrier.
Adherence: set SMART goals (specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound), so progress can be judged and goals stay realistic.
Adherence: track progress with an app or diary, so improvement is visible and motivation holds.
Adherence: vary activities, which prevents boredom and reduces overuse injuries.
Adherence: reward milestones, so each achievement gives a reason to continue.
Adherence: plan for barriers such as bad weather or lack of time, with an indoor option or a shorter session, so one bad week does not end the habit.
Adherence: build up gradually to avoid injury and soreness, which can make people stop.
Adherence: join a club or class for social support, which gives people a commitment to others.

notes.b: Significant people include parents and family, PE teachers, coaches, peers, local club volunteers, sports stars and role models.
points: Enthusiastic and passionate about activity, which spreads to the people they work with.
Lead by example by being active themselves.
Positive and encouraging, which builds confidence in people who doubt their ability.
Approachable and supportive, so people feel comfortable asking for help.
Knowledgeable about the activity and about how to teach or coach it safely.
Inclusive and fair to all abilities, so everyone feels welcome.
Reliable and committed, so people can count on them to turn up.
Good communicators who explain clearly and give useful feedback.
Visible and relatable to the target group, so people see someone like themselves taking part.
Role models inspire people to try an activity they might not otherwise consider.
Role models show that taking part is possible for 'people like me'.
Role models raise the profile of a sport and bring it to the attention of new players and families.

questions.prompt: Name a national policy that promotes physical activity and analyse how it promotes physical activity engagement.
questions.model: The National Physical Activity Plan for Ireland, published in 2016, aims to increase physical activity levels across the population. It promotes engagement by setting out actions across health, education, transport, sport and communities, so more people are encouraged to be active in settings such as school, work and their local area. Its cross-sector approach is a strength, because coordinated action across government sectors can reach people in several settings at once, and a shared national framework gives local bodies such as clubs, schools and councils a common direction. Its limitations are that delivery depends on each sector implementing its actions, so gaps in implementation or funding can slow progress locally, and many community actions rely on volunteers, which limits how far they can expand.

questions.prompt: Discuss how a named National Governing Body supports the development of its sport at local level.
questions.model: The GAA, the governing body for Gaelic football and hurling, supports development at local level in several ways. It affiliates clubs and gives them governance, insurance, safeguarding policies and codes of conduct, so clubs can run safely and to a common standard. It educates coaches, officials and first-aiders, so each club has people able to teach and officiate. Development officers work with schools and clubs to introduce pupils to the games and link them to local clubs. Local leagues and blitzes give beginners and young players regular, low-pressure games that keep them involved. Grants for facilities and equipment reduce the cost barrier, so clubs can improve their grounds and buy kit. Together these supports build the club base from which players progress.

questions.prompt: Outline three characteristics of significant people, such as role models, who promote participation among young people.
questions.model: 1. Enthusiastic and passionate: a significant person who is enthusiastic about activity spreads that enthusiasm to others and makes taking part appealing. 2. Leads by example: being active themselves shows young people that activity is normal and achievable. 3. Positive and encouraging: praise and support build the confidence of young people who doubt their own ability, so they keep trying.
